'''''Encephalartos altensteinii''''' is a species of [[Arecaceae|palm]]-like [[cycad]] in the family [[Zamiaceae]]. It is endemic to [[South Africa]]. The species name ''altensteinii'' commemorates [[Karl vom Stein zum Altenstein|Altenstein]], a 19th-century German chancellor and patron of science.<ref name="CO">{{Cite web|url=http://www.conifers.org/za/Encephalartos_altensteinii.php|title=Encephalartos altensteinii () description|website=www.conifers.org|access-date=2017-08-01}}</ref> It is commonly known as the '''breadtree''', '''broodboom''', '''Eastern Cape giant cycad''' or '''uJobane''' ([[Zulu language|Zulu]]).<ref name="PP">Palmer, E. and Pitman, N. ''Trees of Southern Africa''. Cape Town (1972).</ref> It is listed as vulnerable due to [[habitat destruction]], use for traditional medicine and removal by collectors.<ref name=IUCN/>

This cycad grows up to {{convert|7|m|spell=in}} tall and may be branched or unbranched. The leaves are straight or curved backwards and up to {{convert|3|m|spell=in}} in length. The leaflets are rigid and fairly broad with one or both margins toothed. There are no prickles at the base of the leaf which distinguishes it from ''E. natalensis''. There are usually two to five greenish-yellow cones up to {{convert|50|cm}} long, the female scales covered with protuberances. The cones are poisonous to humans.<ref>[http://www.ourcivilisation.com/smartboard/shop/reitzd/commando/index.htm Deneys Reitz. Commando: A Boer Journal Of The Boer War], chapter 22, "Moss-Troopers", first published by Faber and Faber in Great Britain in 1929, {{ISBN|0-571-08778-7}}</ref> The seeds are scarlet and up to {{convert|4|cm|spell=in}} long.<ref name="PP"/>

==Distribution and habitat==
This species is widespread in the Eastern Cape and south-western KwaZulu-Natal provinces of [[South Africa]]. It favours sites near the coast including open scrub, steep rocky slopes, evergreen forests in valleys<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://plantnet.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/cgi-bin/cycadpg?taxname=Encephalartos+altensteinii|title=Encephalartos altensteinii|website=plantnet.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au|access-date=2017-08-01|archive-date=2016-03-04|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160304052540/http://plantnet.rbgsyd.nsw.gov.au/cgi-bin/cycadpg?taxname=Encephalartos+altensteinii}}</ref> and river banks. It also occurs inland at a higher altitude in isolated sites in the [[Amatola Mountains]].<ref name=IUCN/>

The individual growing in the [[Palm House, Kew Gardens|Palm House]] at [[Kew Gardens|Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew]], UK is considered to be the oldest potted plant in the world, having arrived there in 1775.<ref name="Avis-Riordan2019">{{cite web |last1=Avis-Riordan |first1=Katy |title=Meet the oldest pot plant in the world |url=https://www.kew.org/read-and-watch/oldest-pot-plant-in-world-eastern-cape-giant-cycad |website=Royal Botanic Gardens Kew |access-date=23 June 2023}}</ref> Other individuals have also reached a great age, with the one in [[Lednice–Valtice Cultural Landscape|Lednice Greenhouse]], Czech Republic estimated to be 300 to 600 years old.<ref name="Cykasy">{{cite web |title=Encephalartos Altensteinii in Lednice Chateau Greenhouse |url=http://www.cykasy.cz/English/Lednice_Greenhouse.html |website=Cykasy - Czech cycads |access-date=23 June 2023}}</ref><ref name="Hodgkiss2018">{{cite web |last1=Hodgkiss |first1=R. J. |title=The Cycad page – Cycadaceae, Stangeriaceae, Zamiaceae |url=https://succulent-plant.com/families/cycadaceae.html |website=The Succulent Plant page}}</ref>
